entry.title: What Strategist Readers Bought This Month: Lots of Poplights
entry.summary: Plus fancy cinnamon, Advent calendars, and fall footwear.
entry.content:
Welcome back to “Your Shopping Cart,” where we break out the top products that you, devoted Strategist readers, bought in droves. Think of this as the TL;DR of the Strategist. If your like-minded fellow readers are buying these items, maybe you’d like to as well.

I am charmed by the fact that many of you have been contemplating the purchase of fancy cinnamon. For those who do end up getting some, I recommend making the Smitten Kitchen pumpkin bread with it. Another cozy fall purchase being saved for later was Poplight, the renter-friendly stick-on sconce that interior designers recommend for gloomy hallways.

As for which items you clicked through to learn more about, Bonne Maman’s much-anticipated Advent calendar was a predictable hit, alongside the Anthropologie calendar that also drew lots of interest when it launched back in September. It’s less than a month until you get to start opening those windows. And not only did many of you save the Poplight for later — many of you clicked through in advance of the end of daylight saving time.

Read more: The 10 Best What I Can’t Live Withouts

Beauty Brief readers heard it first: Senescence is a word you’re soon going to be seeing everywhere in anti-aging-product marketing. (It’s basically just a fancy way of saying “growing old.”) Marie Veronique is one of the latest brands to hop on the trend with its new Senolytic Series, which includes a balm and serum that are supposed to target cell longevity.

Want more? Sign up for The Strategist Beauty Brief here.

“Practicing patience is one of my greatest parenting struggles, especially when I’m overstimulated or have to listen to someone chew,” our senior editor Jen Trolio admitted this month to readers of The Strategist Kids’ Department. “So I’m a little in awe of anyone who’s able to joyfully cook alongside a toddler; sure, they are wonderfully and endlessly curious, but they’re also clumsy and prone to outbursts that don’t mix well with knives and forks.” Two people who have mastered this patient art? Kristen Miglore and Junnifa Uzodike, two Montessori experts who’ve written a guide to setting up your kitchen — and shifting your mind-set — to successfully make food with your kids.

Want more? Sign up for The Strategist Kids’ Department here.

Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens recently ordered this double-walled borosilicate-glass travel mug. And while it can’t compete with stainless steel for maintaining piping-hotness, it keeps drinks warm (preheating with boiling water helps) and is completely plastic-free. It’s a pleasure to sip from and, as she puts it, a “good gift for a certain type of person.”

For The Strategist Daily, several longtime writers and editors looked back on their most revelatory purchases from the site over the past ten years. For senior writer Lauren Ro, these sliding chip clips came to mind: “My husband read about them on the Strategist and ordered them immediately. We still use them every single day. They’re the best at keeping snacks and other foods fresh. I can’t believe we’ve had them for six years.”

entry.title: What Nulastin Founder Leah Garcia Buys at the Drugstore
entry.summary: “When I travel, I pour some into the little bottles of hotel-room lotion. It makes it feel luxurious.”
entry.content:
Here at the Strategist, we love hearing about everyday stuff that actually works. That line of thinking extends to the drugstore beauty products in our medicine cabinets, shower caddies, and makeup bags. In our series “Beauty Aisle,” we talk to folks in the beauty industry — aestheticians, hairstylists, makeup artists, dermatologists, and the like — about the go-to affordable products they keep stocked. For this installment, writer Arielle Avila chatted with Nulastin founder Leah Garcia about the drugstore products she loves.

First of all, let me just say this: I am annoyed with the soft cotton end of the swab these days. When I was younger, Q-tips had the softest, fluffiest swab. I’m telling you, I think they changed it. Now, I’m still completely devoted to the brand Q-tips. Why? Same reason why I buy Kleenex, but I’m annoyed. I’m constantly looking for one, so I keep them everywhere. It’s probably the least glamorous thing in my beauty routine, but I’m never without them. I use them to clean up the lash line. The only thing I don’t use it for is if I get mascara on my eyelids. Instead, use a spoolie brush to take it off, especially if you’ve already done your eyeshadow. I learned that from Jamie Greenberg on one of her Instagrams. It takes it right off.

I try to wear sunscreen every single day, and I’m particularly diligent about putting it above and around my brows. Sunglasses don’t always protect that area, and I’ve seen so many women experience brow thinning as they get older. After going through changes in my own hair and brows, it’s an area I’m very conscious about protecting. This is literally my favorite sunscreen in the world. I love the small tip applicator. Now, that being said, I’m on my way to Croatia Wednesday, and I will pick up that same sunscreen, but with BEMT, which is the ingredient that just got approved here in the United States. The sunscreen formulation there is different from the U.S. Same brand, just next-level good. But if I’m in the States and I don’t get to poach a product from Europe, then I will go right into Target and pick this one up. It’s non-comedogenic. I don’t get any acne. It disappears after I’ve put it on.

My God, it’s dreamy. This was given to me as a gift at a conference, and now I’m a junkie. I will get it anywhere if I can. This is something I picked up from childhood. My mom used to use old-school baby oil and blend it with some generic lotion. It gives you a nice glistening glow. Now, I use this every time I shower. And when I travel, I pour some into the little bottles of hotel-room lotion. Those lotions never seem to moisturize at all. But you add this, and now all of a sudden you’ve got whatever generic lotion from a hotel room mixed with that Saltair. It makes it feel luxurious.

Listen, I normally will pick Native because I like the way it looks on my counter. No question. It’s not because I put it on, I go, “Oh, that’s really great.” As a matter of fact, I don’t think I’ve ever read their ingredient deck. It might have dimethicone in it for all I know, which I’ve been trying to avoid. But I buy it first for what it looks like on my counter, which is not right. So my tip would be, read the directions. If you need to adjust, adjust. But I figured that was better than Vaseline, in terms of body lotion. I am a creature of my past, so it’s either Lubriderm, Eucerin, any of those, but I just want a clean, usually white bottle on my vanity. That’s what I’m after.

Who can win with their heels? It’s like pushing the biggest boulder up a hill. No matter how many times I try to get all that calluses off of it, it’s just fighting back. I think the whole thing is disgusting, so I buy new foot files whenever I can. I don’t want that shit reused. I don’t want to be like, “Oh, where’s that heel scrubber from four years ago?” I just get a new one. They’re not that precious. Mine has one of those notches, so that all your little callus junk stays in there. I can’t let all that dead skin go flying everywhere either.

I used to love Crest. I then got told by somebody at one point to use Sensodyne. My husband and I both couldn’t stand the smell of either. I think when you get older, your sense of smell changes and affects what you can and can’t tolerate. I’ve also tried to go into Whole Foods and get some of their toothpaste. First of all, it’s full of air. It looks like a big toothpaste, but it’s not. Then, you use it, and you have to use a lot of it, because it really doesn’t feel like it does much. The consistency feels overly whipped. I can afford to go try these new things, but I feel very strongly that I don’t get nickeled and dimed like a potato chip bag that has a very small amount. I want to get my money’s worth with things like toothpaste. Finally, we switched to Colgate. It’s not the typical one, but a slightly more expensive, bougier one. This Colgate will last me forever.

I don’t mind sweating, but I do mind smelling. Old Spice is a deodorant but not an antiperspirant, so it doesn’t stop sweating. Years ago I was told it’s best not to use antiperspirants, so I’ve just stuck to that. I’ve been using this because it’s easy. Plus, I can share it with my man.

I’ve never missed a day of flossing in the last 35 years. Listen, I don’t know if it’s environmentally really friendly for all of us to be using these, but they are made from recycled plastic. I love the dual floss string as opposed to just the single string. One string will break, and all of the reviews that you see are accurate. A game-changer is that once you get done with the string side‚ you flip down the end of it, and then the other end is a pick to get up into your gums. It’s a process, but it feels really good. My husband and I affectionately call them harpsichords, even though it’s not even shaped like a harpsichord. I don’t know why, but we say, “Did you pack your harpsichord?”

I don’t wash my hair every day; I wash about every fourth day. On those days I need to throw my hair in a fun bun, I use a scrunchie. I can’t even use an old school ponytail holder anymore. It has to have a soft silk or cotton around it. I’m not particular about the brand, I just like something soft and easy that I can throw my hair up with without fussing over it. I loan them out all the time to my friends, so I’m constantly having to buy new ones.

entry.title: What Erika Alexander Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “I recently bought Hillary Clinton some stationery from there.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. We asked actress and comedian Erika Alexander — who stars in season two of The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins — about the scalp oil, cotton T-shirts, and body butter she can’t live without.

So a lot of people have been talking about bonnets and whether they are appropriate and all of those things. But for many years, people have been wearing scarves. I think there’s a kind of renewed interest in scarves, not just from a cultural point of view, but from a reference of those in the Deco period; they always wore these beautiful scarves. It didn’t matter what color you were or where you were from. And so this is kind of a nod to the beauty of those scarves, but she adds wire to make it sculptural. So when I’m not having my hair in a wig or anything on, how can I look really coiffed? I grab that silk scarf and I wire it up, put some earrings on, and I look like I’m ready to shop or get on a plane.
And the silk, of course, is good for preventing breakage in my hair. I love it. Ashaka Givens also used to be Erykah Badu’s hatter.

The Gymwrap is by my friend Nicole Ari Parker. Again, there’s emphasis on my hair and laying these edges down, but also making sure so they don’t break. Having edges at this age especially is a result of wrapping my hair up at night. But when you sweat and you go to the gym, you need something to not only catch the sweat but to keep the hair from getting wet. It will start to draw down. But it doesn’t do that with this. And it’s successful for Nicole. She’s an actress like me. I really love that she’s an entrepreneur. It actually works.
I don’t just put it on when I’m walking or working out. I put it on the shower to protect from the mist and humidity. I’ll also wear it to travel, and I’ll wear it with Akash’s scarf on so I don’t get any of the oil and stuff on my scarf. I’ll put it on as an in-between thing.

I went into Pineider’s Rockefeller Center boutique after noticing it had beautiful leathers. I bought quite a few bags, and one of them was this shoulder bag in a beautiful orange, which I like. I’m really trying to be conscious now and not just buy a bag because it’s expensive or has a logo.

And it turns out that they not only do bags, but they do pens and stationery too, and I love to write. My favorite pen is a beautiful ballpoint pen that has enamel on it and gold tongue. I now buy all my stationery and gifts from there. I recently bought Hillary Clinton some stationery from there, which I have to send to her because it was just her birthday. She’s one of my mentors in life. And of course, she would appreciate it because I’ve gotten so many thank you letters from her that were written by her and signed by her. I think she’s old school in a way that she understands that people don’t often send correspondence that way, but one of the most precious things I have is my stack of letters from her.

[While Erika didn’t specify which stationery item from Pineider she likes the most, we’ve linked to a similar item on its site here.]

I met the co-founder Stephen Satterfield while he was hosting the Netflix series High on the Hog. After that gig he went into sourcing cotton after hearing about Black farmers who didn’t know how to distribute their cotton. So he created Comoco T-shirts so they could have a place to put their cotton. It’s fantastic. They have both a white and black T-shirt. I love it, and think people should know about it, because it’s actually beautiful cotton. It’s made here in America, and you’re supporting farmers and Black people in the South.

I get the small, but I think that you should order a little bigger because I don’t think it’s preshrunk.

About five or six years ago, I was at Brooklyn Bowl and learned about this body butter from the Black women working at the shoe rental counter. She had a bottle of Don’t Be Ashy next to her on the counter, which turned out to be her side business. I bought a couple, because I like to buy things to give when I visit people on Broadway, whether it’s Audra McDonald, Joy Reid, or Nikole Hannah Jones. I’ve now given several people Don’t Be Ashy. You can’t beat this body butter. It’s the best.

My makeup artist, Frederick Sanders, uses a bunch of different things, but I find that on me, this deep red, Bawse Lady, just happens to be a really pretty red, especially on my skin, which has a lot of red in it. This has a little blue in it. It’s really nice and deep and sexy and bright. I also like the name of it.

I discovered this at one of my favorite shops, Layla, in Brooklyn. The perfume itself is from a Los Angeles perfumer, Leanne Hirsh, who makes natural colognes with natural ingredients. Beautiful, unique smells. Choita is what sent me to her. It’s really nice, not sweet or musky. It’s got a good balance. It smells like you’re in an inn, somewhere in New Hampshire or someplace that’s kind of old and worn, but bright, because it’s got a woodiness. But I like sweet smells, so I can smell that there too.

She also gives perfume-making classes. So I took a class with her, and now I’ve made my own perfume called Maverick. I then just went down the rabbit hole with her. She’s fantastic, and I just love everything she does, but this is my favorite perfume from her.

I buy people these robes when I don’t know what to give them. These are also from my favorite shop Layla’s. When my boyfriend was losing his mother, his two aunties were there and were always sitting on the couch in their clothes. So I said, “I’m gonna get them these robes.” And they lived in those robes while she passed away. They’re hand-blocked, cotton, and prewashed. They turned out to be perfect for them, and they still love them. I have one too, but I love to give them as well.

This is a dress you could put on a president or an empress. It’s just beautiful and I love the way it hinges at the hips. It’s a dress that you can wear anywhere. I like to wear it for press and speaking engagements. This color is a good color; it’s not a hard red, it’s kind of a saffron red. I also just love the way Sergio makes clothes. I love his story. I like the way he came into fashion and built something for himself, and all the word of mouth on him meets the moment. He’s a good man who knows how to make clothes.

I spend a lot of time dealing with my hair. On my current set I have Nray Locs, so I have to oil my scalp a lot, but it can’t look too oily. This oil is perfect. My hairdresser for The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, Roseline Davies, who’s Liberian American, created it. It’s just soft enough to get in my hair and oil the scalp, but it’s not greasy. Also, I need a healthy scalp. There’s a lot that’s happening to it every day. A lot of attention, especially as an actor, is on my hair and my scalp. It gets so much abuse trying to stay natural and also trying to be trendy. This is perfect.

entry.title: We Stopped 57 New Yorkers to Ask About Their Fall Shoes
entry.summary: Flats, loafers, and boots galore.
entry.content:
Now that temperatures have dipped in New York, open-toe season has come to a close. Sandals have swapped in for boots, loafers, and other cold-weather fare. Curious about what shoes New Yorkers are wearing this season, three Strategist writers canvassed the city, stopping people on street corners in the Flatiron District, Fort Greene, and the Upper East Side. We approached people on their way to the office, while they drank their afternoon coffees, as they were walking their dogs, and right before they hopped into an Uber with their groceries. We asked about comfortability and wearability, nodding knowingly when they gushed about the magic of zippers, blister-free leather, and the enduring appeal of Frye boots.

Ballet flats abounded in various heel heights, loafers showed up in different shapes and colors, and leathers, suedes, and croc-esque textures were on display. And as was the case when we asked New Yorkers about their work bags, plenty of secondhand and vintage finds sourced from eBay and Poshmark were in the mix, too. Below are all the shoes we spotted, shared with the permission — and thoughts — of their wearers.

“I’ve worn these Jeffrey Careful shoes for the past three months. They’re pretty much broken in; I wear them 24/7. I have a little bit of a bunion and they don’t bother me at all, or on the back of my ankle. They’re suede and leather and kind of like Tabis, which many of my friends have and need to resole. You can see the bottoms here — I’ve worn them a lot, and especially against New York City concrete sidewalks, the soles still look really good.”

“I got these in the Netherlands at the Posa store. I think they’re very cute — you can combine them with everything; that’s why I love them. And they’re very comfortable. I’ve had them for two months. I wear them to study, and yesterday, I walked 30,000 steps in them without any blisters or anything.”

“I love these because they are suede and very comfortable. I bought them about a year ago, actually. Straight out of the box, I wore them without any blisters. I walk a lot and wear these a lot, two to three miles at a time, and they still look pretty great.”

“The shoes are by a former ’70s Japanese brand called Haruta. I acquired them at Front General Store in Brooklyn. They’re super comfortable. I’ve owned them for about two years, but the wear on them does not reflect that.”

“I bought these in Park City, Utah. They’ve been interesting. It took me a little while to get used to them, but I like them now that I’ve broken them in. They feel sleek and cool.”

“I bought these on the RealReal. They took some breaking in and I had to add a thing in the back to make them more comfortable, but now I wear them all the time.”

“I wear them everywhere. Whenever I travel, I bring them because you can pair them with a casual fit but you can also dress them up.”

“I saw these in an ad and Google reverse-image searched. We were comparing them to Tabis last night. They’re Tabi-shaped but without the indentations.”

“I usually buy expensive shoes, but I took a chance on these. They’re from Zara, so I don’t know how long they’ll last. I got them in Paris.”

“I’ve had these for three months. They’re super comfortable. No break-in period. Daily 10,000 steps are no problem, and the most I’ve done in them is 25,000. I haven’t put on my Salomon sneakers in a very long time because of that. The cut in the front reminded me of the Loro Piana flat, which I wanted for so long. The rubber on these makes them really great for walking because I feel like they’re absorbing some of it. I love the little V in the front and the square toe. I think it’s, like, a really elegant shape.”

“I’ve had these for two seasons now. I also got them in tan suede. They come in a lot of different colors, and they’re really very comfortable for walking in the city. No blisters or breaking in — absolutely nothing. I think I may be getting them in burgundy. They’re so comfortable. Just put them on and go.”

“These are suede loafers from G.H.Bass, and I actually bought them recently. I was looking for something that looked nicer than a beat-up sneaker. They’re comfortable and I can slip them on easily when I’m walking my dog, Banchan.”

“I’m obsessed with them. It’s this French brand called Soeur. I wore them all summer long. I wear them almost every day. You can hike, you can run, you can dance, you can do anything — no issues. I want them to last forever.”

“I got them from the Korner. I’m from Hong Kong, and they’re a very popular Hong Kong brand. I love how versatile and comfortable they are. I wear them to conferences, work events, and also just on a nice Sunday afternoon. I’m usually in scrubs and Crocs, so it’s nice to wear something more cute.”

“I actually just got these yesterday from Asos. I work in a corporate office, so I’m trying to be professional but make it a little bit more fun.”

“They took a while to break it. I have another pair of Tony Bianco boots that were way more comfortable. These took maybe 15 times wearing them. I also went to town with a hair dryer. But now they are like slippers. Anytime where I used to wear a sneaker, now I wear these.”

“I was on the hunt for a long time for the perfect loafer. I saw these at a store in Easthampton and I was like, Okay, wait, these actually look exactly like the shoes that I want, because I wanted them to be comfortable and something that I can wear all the time. I’ve had them for a few months now, and they’ve stretched to my foot nicely because I’m walking everywhere. It’s been a perfect, comfortable everyday shoe. People think they’re The Row.”

“I’ve had these for years. They’re cute little pony-hair slingback flats from Schutz. They’re just so easy to slip on when I walk my dog. They look like slippers, right? But they have an elastic slingback. You’re the third person to compliment me on them. The thing is it’s a little bit of a conundrum sometimes because it has to be the exact right temperature. They’re sherpa-lined, so it can’t be too hot, but if it’s a little bit too chilly, like it was this morning, then I need to put socks on.”

“I was at a Buffalo Exchange in the Bay Area and saw these brown oiled Danskos and knew I had to add them to my Dansko collection. I have three pairs total: classic black, these brown, and a calf-leather kind of furry pair that people really love. I love the arch support. I love that you can kick them on and kick them off super easily. They’re heavy in the rotation. I will say the thing with Danskos is, for people who are not used to them, you have to figure out how to walk in them a little bit because of the platform. You have to be careful, or you will stumble. The city can be a little precarious for a Dansko wearer.”

“These are from a Japanese company called Hender Scheme, and they’re leather craftspeople. They normally make very simple, basic leather shoes, and then these were just a crazy mash-up that I thought were so exciting and had never seen before. This was my first purchase from the brand. I had been waiting for the diamond in the rough. They are incredible. Their craft and their quality as a maker in the shoe space really stands out.”

“These are Arc’teryx slide-on shoes. If you’re ever going climbing outside, they’re grippy for the mountain leading up to your climb. They’re also really comfortable and go with everything.”

“I’m wearing these amazing knee-high — I’d say white — boots from Frances Valentine. They’re literally so comfortable. They have a little block kitten heel. I have been wearing them for a few hours and could walk all around all day. I feel like the designer really knows what she’s doing. I mean, she knows that women in New York walk. I just got them for fall, like, a week ago. This is also the first time I’m wearing them, so this is the break-in walk, and I’m totally fine. I got them in red too. I’m very happy. They’re a good heel height too — not too high, not too short. Once it gets colder, I feel like it’ll look cute under pants also, so they’re really versatile.”

“These are my Steve Madden cowboy boots — but they have a zipper on the side, so they’re very easy to put on, not like a classic cowboy boot. I’ve had this shoe for, like, four years, and this is my second pair because they just wear in the heel a little bit. I loved them so much that I bought them again. They’re extremely comfortable. I walk very fast — like, I’m booking it getting on the subway — and I’m tall; I’m 5’9. So I feel like I’m naturally faster than people and step harder than people. So these wear well. I have to get another pair soon.”

“These are my party shoes. I’ve had them for over a year now, and they’re cute. I like that the fabric goes over the boot.”

“These are comfortable and easy to walk in. I also like that they zip on the side, so you don’t have to worry about the shoe strings.”

I just got these, they’re Sam Edelman. They’re brown leather and very cute.

“These are dupe Frye boots — like, 60 bucks on Amazon. We’ve been beep-bopping all day, no pain. Super comfy, would recommend!”

“I spent way too much money on these, but unfortunately, I love them. I wanted to hate them so I could return them and not feel guilty. I’m thankful for Afterpay.”

“I found these on Farfetch. I bought them on sale and still paid too much for them, but I love them so much. An Everywoman’s witchy October boot.”

I was going to get them in another color, but I wear a half-size, and they stopped carrying 6.5.”

As most vintage shoes are no longer available, we included a few alternates for each pair.

“I have owned these for nine years and worn them across the country. I love them so much; they’re my best friends.”

I think that they’re pretty true to size. I do have a pretty bony foot, so thick socks are always a must for me — but with a thick sock, they do the job.”

“I thrifted these. Once it’s fall, I’m always excited to break my boots out. I was kind of rushing over here for work. So I said, What’s going to get me to and from while also maintaining some level of style? These are just always easy to wear. It’s nice to know that I can always come back to these. They’re classic.”

The listing said they were handmade in Mexico. They are magic. I’ve walked 20 miles in Manhattan in them. They literally go with everything. My feet are a size 11, so every time I’m looking for shoes, especially on websites like eBay, I always just put my size in the search term because I’ll take whatever I can get. entry.title: How to Get the Most Out of Nuuly, According to Nuulyologists
entry.summary: If you have limited closet space or just attended a lot of weddings this year, then you’ve probably heard of the clothing-rental service Nuuly.
entry.content:
If you’re a frequent shopper who can’t resist a new arrivals rack, is trying to cut down on the amount of clothes you buy, struggles with limited closet space, or has just attended a lot of weddings this year, then you’ve probably heard of Nuuly. For $98 a month (and $70 for first timers with a code), the clothing-rental service lets you borrow six items from brands like Free People, Hill House, Anthropologie, Farm Rio, Damson Madder, and Lisa Says Gah. You can pick everything from dresses, coats, and jeans to T-shirts and sweatshirts to wear and return ahead of your next billing date, when you unlock your next six items. The rental service offers one membership built around six items, but you can customize on a monthly basis by adding bonus items for $22. If you fall in love with an item (or multiple) from your bag, the service also gives you the option to purchase the item at a discount or buy it directly from the Nuuly Thrift Shop and it add to your monthly order.

As a Nuuly user of nearly two years, my favorite things about the service — besides the fact that I don’t have to be responsible for washing the items I rent — have been the opportunity to play around with my personal style and to save money and space in my closet by renting bigger items such as formalwear, coats, and jackets. But making the most of my subscription and finding the best picks every month can feel overwhelming, especially when the items need to be available in my size and be likely to actually fit. With this in mind, I spoke to four longtime Nuuly users around the city to get their best advice for renting clothes on the platform.

Choosing what to rent from Nuuly starts with building a Closet, a wish-list-adjacent feature where users can save items in one place and start planning selections for each month. Temi Omilabu, a New York lawyer who’s been using Nuuly for two years, recommends scrolling through Nuuly’s “Just For You” page — a personalized section of the site that recommends items based on your browsing history and saved items — if you don’t know where to start.

Nuuly adds new clothing to the site on a rolling basis and does not have a public calendar revealing when new items are dropping. While this is somewhat of an equalizer — no shopper is at an advantage or disadvantage based on their billing date or schedule — it can also prevent you from feeling totally in control of your monthly order. Kelsey Horowitz, a Brooklyn-based therapist who has been using Nuuly for about two years, recommends filtering for the newest items and browsing on a weekly basis to stay on top of the site’s offerings. As with any rental site, newer items will be less worn. “The trade-off is that if you want to buy anything, it’s not as discounted,” says McCormick.

After adding items to a Closet, users can organize further using Lists, which allow you to sort your Closet into categories. Ivy Peterson, a brand-strategy manager based in Manhattan who’s been using Nuuly for five years, saves items in her closet, then makes her actual lists based on what’s in her calendar for the next few weeks. “I look at my entire month and see what I have coming up — maybe I have a wedding, a date night, or just a lot of work stuff,” Peterson says. “I get the lay of the land and write down in my Notes app ‘One formal dress, two pairs of pants, three fun tops,’ just to give myself something to start with.” You can also use Lists to pin seasonal items, vacation outfits, and special-event outfit ideas in groups for later so you avoid scrambling when it comes time to plan your bag.

No matter how much time you spend preparing, there’s a chance the items you save will be out of stock when you need them most. Nuuly does not alert you when an item you’ve saved comes back in stock, but it does offer alternatives. “That has happened to me a handful of times, and it’s heartbreaking, so just save backups,” Omilabu says. “Nuuly’s algorithm is pretty good at pointing you in a different direction.” When you’re actually picking out your items, you can filter your Closet using the “Available Now” button so you’re only seeing options that are ready to rent.

Nuuly is a great way to try pieces that are otherwise hit or miss for sizing. Casey McCormick, a creative strategist who has been using Nuuly for seven years, started using it to learn about brands that cater to plus sizes. “I love Fashion Brand Company,” says McCormick. “I got a T-shirt from them because it had fun embroidered cigarettes on it, and it was so soft.” Since then, she’s rented more pieces from the brand, including a Bikini Bod T-Shirt Dress. Longtime Nuuly users agree that jeans are particularly worth trying on the app. Peterson has only bought three things in her five years on Nuuly, and they were all jeans. “Jeans are really hard for me,” Peterson explains. “I think I rented each of them four or five times, then I was like, All right, these are mine.” In that moment, she decided to purchase them from the site.

“Coats and outerwear are one of my favorite types of apparel, but I don’t have a coat closet,” says McCormick. “If I had my way, I would have a massive walk-in closet filled with beautiful coats. So I try to replicate the feeling by getting different stuff throughout the winter seasons or colder seasons through Nuuly.” Peterson, who skis in the winter but has nowhere in her apartment to store bulky clothing, hasn’t bought a coat in five years but has rented many. Some of her favorites include the Barogodo Ski Jacket from Farm Rio, the Cropped ’90s Ski Puffer from Champion, and the Nightfall Quilted Puffer from Sadie & Sage.

Similar to traditional online shopping, it can be hard to tell the quality of an item before ordering. The Nuuly reviews — which are uniquely photo heavy and typically include notes on quality or fit — can really help. “Sizing for women’s clothing in general is bananas, but for plus-size women in particular, it’s so wildly inconsistent,” explains McCormick. “I specifically look for people [in the reviews] who are my size, who look like me, and who carry weight like I do because even with brands you trust, every garment is different.” The reviews also help flag clothing-rental-specific issues, like if certain items show more noticeable wear (fabric piling, color fading, etc.). If an item in your order arrives in poor condition, the Nuuly customer-service team is usually helpful and will generally offer a bonus item or a discount on your next order.

The most structured way to use Nuuly is to rent six items every month and return them ahead of your next billing date to unlock your next bag. You can, however, technically keep your items past the billing date, then return when you’re actually ready for your next bag — even if that’s two weeks into your next month. You’ll still be charged monthly for your membership, but that membership entitles you to keep items longer, postpone your UPS Store run, and return items late if your billing date doesn’t line up perfectly with your special-events calendar.

Whether you’re using Nuuly specifically to try items before you buy them or to never have to purchase another item again, it’s important to know that buying is an option. Anything you rent on Nuuly is available for purchase and everything is discounted, sometimes up to 75 percent off the retail price. (Discounts are offered on an item-by-item basis using factors Nuuly doesn’t disclose.) The service also frequently offers discount codes that provide $10 or $20 off a purchase, which can be used in addition to the existing discount.

Final-sale Nuuly items are also available for purchase on Nuuly’s Thrift Shop, which is only available to subscribers. Purchases from the Thrift Shop are shipped alongside monthly rentals at no additional shipping cost and do not count against the six items unlocked with a subscription. Many of the stores Nuuly partners with, including Anthropologie, Free People, and Urban Outfitters, also sell retired rentals from Nuuly directly on their websites.

entry.title: I Hiked for 14 Days to Find the Best-Tasting Granola Bar
entry.summary: I wanted a delicious bar with visible, recognizable ingredients that would be easy to eat while walking.
entry.content:
Nestled between “hot air balloon ride” and “meet Martha Stewart,” “hike the Camino Primitivo” has been at the top of my bucket list for years. This fall, I finally crossed off the last, (and if anyone reading this has a hot air balloon or is Martha Stewart, please do not hesitate to reach out.) The Camino Primitivo is a 9th-century pilgrimage route from Oviedo to Santiago de Compostela, Spain, winding 200 miles through scenic valleys, remote villages, and more cows than a girl could dare to dream of. After booking my flight and making sure my boots still fit, I addressed my next natural priority: snacks.

When it comes to trail food, there is still no substitute for the granola bar. But in the fracas of the global protein explosion and the science-ification of Good Old Raisins and Peanuts, we’ve lost the folk soul inherent to what it means to be “crunchy.” So in tandem with my pilgrimage through Asturias and Galicia came a different kind of spiritual quest: to find the granola bar’s platonic ideal.

I want a bar with visible, recognizable ingredients. I want to be able to see the oats and nuts, and I want a recipe that I can feasibly recreate in my own kitchen. I want something that evokes the comfort inherent to the granola bars I grew up eating — the Nature Valley pulled out of my mom’s purse on road trips, the requisite Quaker Chewy inhaled after a rec soccer game — and that’s an antidote to the blocks of -gyns and -ates that fill every grocery store aisle today.

As I’d be taking these bars for long walking days I needed them to be hearty and filling with nutritional elements that make me feel prudent and responsible. I am neither a registered dietician nor a high-performance athlete, so these metrics are malleable to me, but I know to look for a balance of carbs, a few grams of fiber, protein, and minimal added sugar. I’d also need them to be formulated for eating on the move — if more of every bite’s landing on the trail than in my mouth, we’re toast. Especially considering, most essentially, I’m looking for a bar that tastes amazing.

So, for every day of my two-week hike I sampled a different granola bar, and I found all the best that GORP can be.

Protein: 7 grams / Fiber: 4 grams / Carbohydrates: 27 grams

This is a bar with a point of view! The only savory option on this list, the earthy flavors of turmeric and garlic rounded out with hints of date and agave nectar were a very welcome respite from a glut of chocolate chips in the other bars I sampled. In keeping with its “we do things a little different here” vibe, the package opens on the long edge, not the top. This one keeps you guessing!

For all its ingenuity and truly amazing flavor, though, whole peanuts and coconut flakes make this bar a little on the crumbly side. It’s better enjoyed stationary, maybe seated on a rock overlooking a gorgeous vista where you can think about how life is full of surprises, and you’re holding one of them.

Protein: 4 grams / Fiber: 5 grams / Carbohydrates: 32 grams

I’ve always had a soft spot for this brand because candidly I have a crush on the guitar-wielding Dave drawn in the logo, looking like the Fabio of whole grain bread. I gave him a little kiss before opening the wrapper to find this bar had turned into crumbs in my backpack, broken up into sweet little morsels like the topping of a blueberry crumble.

Its ingredients list is longer than others in my lineup, with things I’d never buy unless I was having an organic vegetable glycerin-themed party or something. But every broken bite was delicious — the sweetest by far, with a flavor not unlike a British flapjack, right down to the whole oats. Though not a bar that maintains its integrity when packed and smushed, I would gladly have it with a cup of coffee as a special treat, and I’m not just talking about cartoon Dave’s bulging bicep.

Protein: 10 grams / Fiber: 4 grams / Carbohydrates: 29 grams

I’ve loved RXBARs ever since my family got a Costco membership, but I have countless friends who can’t stand the things, bemoaning the texture, fretting that they’re too thick and chewy. The addition of peanut butter and rolled oats does away with the divisive density of the originals, adding enough subtle variation to make every bite feel new. Just when you think you know what you’re in for, boom: little pumpkin seed. It still necessitates an athletic bite, but I think that’s a feature, not a bug. Nothing good is ever easy, and lots of chewing gives you more time to meditate on how yummy the honey and cinnamon taste, and how happy you are that there’s not a single crumb falling on the trail.

Protein: 4 grams / Fiber: 5 grams / Carbohydrates: 30 grams

I ate this bar with my butt in a river, feeling grateful that I was tasting something as sweet as the feeling of having my butt in a river. Dates are doing the heavy lifting, making for a soft bite like caramel undercut unmistakingly with banana. At just seven ingredients, all of which you can find at the grocery store, this bar is an impressive feat of chemistry, minimal while still hearty and filling. Kind of exceptionally, none of the seven ingredients are nuts, making this bar largely allergen free. But I found it lacking a little in the texture department — it went down almost too easy.

Protein: 6 grams / Fiber: 2 grams / Carbohydrates: 19 grams

This bar is a work of art. A glistening mosaic of peanuts, raisins, and cacao nibs frozen in a crystalline case of brown rice syrup, almost too beautiful to eat. Bravely, though, I ate it, and it tasted just as good as it looked. A perfect, self-contained snack, like having two handfuls of trail mix without getting your palms all dusty.

It’s the only crunchy bar on my list, a trait that’s hard to come by if you, like me, have sworn off Nature Valley Bars. I ate enough Oat & Honey two-packs in my youth to wrap around the equator if you laid them end to end. This bar’s good enough to almost make me miss them.

Protein: 3 grams / Fiber: 15 grams / Carbohydrates: 29 grams

I will not go into detail because I am a lady, but if you’ve been hiking for a week straight, you know what a beacon of hope “15g fiber” is. Started by the founder of Jeni’s, the Floura bars taste unsurprisingly amazing, especially when they’re aping an essential ice cream flavor. The mint is subtle, but undeniable, commingling with the melange of dried fruits from Floura’s signature plant fiber blend, composed of things like watermelon rinds and apple cores. As such, it’s not a bar I would have the wherewithal to recreate myself, but the ingredients are at least largely words that I recognize.

You have to take your time with this bar. It’s dense and gooey, tiny chia seeds and hemp hearts breaking up every labored chew. But it’s work to which I was happy to apply myself. Lord knows the bar had a job to do, too.

Protein: 6 grams / Fiber: 3 grams / Carbohydrates: 22 grams

If someone told me to draw a granola bar from memory, this is what it would look like. A grade school cafeteria icon all grown up, this 88 Acres snack is a classic, nostalgia-infused chewy oat and chocolate bar wearing her finest jewels, bedazzled with sunflower, pumpkin, and ground flax seeds. Another allergy-friendly option that didn’t give me any trouble while I was eating it in stride.

Protein: 7 grams / Fiber: 3 grams / Carbohydrates: 28 grams

There’s a story written on the wrapper about Bob’s wife lovingly crafting an easy snack of oats, peanut butter, and honey that inspired this bar. Eating it makes me feel like I’m a part of the family. It’s sticky and gooey, kind of like the outside of a banana bread loaf, and it’s made from the mix of ingredients that comprised my breakfast every single day of college, plus tapioca syrup. It’s familiar, no-frills food that works well for walking.

Protein: 4 grams / Fiber: 5 grams / Carbohydrates: 25 grams

Like a classic white T-shirt or the quintessential cashmere turtleneck, this is a bar that believes in simple, minimalist perfection. Its five ingredients are all in a harmonious balance — chewy dates, cacao nibs, chia seeds, and visible chunks of raw almond for texture. The only ingredient I wish I could taste more is the salt, but I think everything is better with more salt. I ate this bar on the move without any fear of deterioration and could have gone for another.

Protein: 9 grams / Fiber: 7 grams / Carbohydrates: 11 grams

Next to caviar, good steak, and the perfect peak-season fig, I believe that one of life’s truest delicacies is the very last dregs of a peanut butter jar. You know, when it gets kind of dry and fudgy and flaky and salty and you have to eat it off the spoon in the dead of night lest someone should see and try to rip it from your hands? This bar is that bite. It’s peanut-buttery and salty and sweet, thanks to the chocolate chips, and features a mix of ingredients like MCT oil and reishi mushroom extract, hence the “superfood” in its name. I cannot confirm whether or not the fact that I felt good while eating this bar had anything to do with the functional ingredients or if it was just because I was eating a yummy bar that I liked, but I can confirm I felt good.

Unlike the bars on this list bound by dates and syrups, its consistency is more chalky than chewy. As such it was a little bit of a mouth workout, but nothing I couldn’t handle, especially with a little water to wash it down.

Protein: 10 grams / Fiber: 5 grams / Carbohydrates: 29 grams

Maybe it’s because I’d been walking for almost two weeks wearing a mammoth backpack (I’d brought Lonesome Dove as my trail book and I swear that tome got heavier every day), but I almost teared up at my first bite of this bar. It tasted just about as much like a peanut butter and jelly as anything that isn’t can hope to, and I happen to think that’s one of the best tastes in the world. With just five ingredients, tied for the fewest of any on this list, this bar’s a magic trick. It’s chewy with big peanut chunks for crunch and organic strawberries in perfect balance. It had masterfully held its shape after 13 days stuffed in my backpack and I ate it practically skipping with joy, no problem. The only reason it didn’t make it on the podium is for the stiff competition between my winners.

Protein: 11 grams / Fiber: 4 grams / Carbohydrates: 20 grams

When I had my first bite of this bar I said “whoa” out loud to no one. It is mind-blowingly delicious and wonderfully sophisticated, flecked with chunks of fig, infused with Masala chai spices and wildflower honey, and riddled with Mission almonds throughout. All ingredients I could find in my pantry if I were a better woman, barring some fibers and protein crisps.
The fact that “peanut butter” is essential enough to feature in the name earns it big points in my book, lending to a consistency at once chewy and cakey. The bites of these handmade bars break off in big chunks, so you have to focus when enjoying it on the move, but I would eat any fallen crumbs off the cold hard ground without even batting an eye.

Protein: 15 grams / Fiber: 15 grams / Carbohydrates: unlisted

I first found this bar at a notoriously hip coffee shop in Manhattan called Cafe Lyria and was immediately intrigued by its lo-fi, handmade packaging. With a masking tape logo and ingredients listed on a sticker, this unassuming bar just begs you to bet against it. But that would be the biggest mistake you ever make in your entire life!

This bar is to die for. It tastes so good. It’s thick and dense, stuffed full of good ingredients like hemp hearts and goji berries and baked to perfection, finished with a salty caramelized top. It’s easy to eat while you’re walking, it’s completely filling and offers impressive nutritional stats with 15 grams of both fiber and protein. I am obsessed with this bar. I want to ask this bar to dance. She’s the prom queen, the most beautiful girl in school, but one that would stand up to bullies and help you with your homework in a cool, humble way.

Protein: 7 grams / Fiber: 4 grams / Carbohydrates: 36 grams

This is a good old fashioned bar. One with family values, one with integrity — what you see is what you get. Whole ingredients announce themselves in every bite, cranberries all but shaking your hand, oats telling you good morning. If this bar were my boyfriend I’d take him home to mama and she would love him as much as I do. It’s perfect for eating and walking, sticky with honey, easy to chew and wholly nourishing. A real meat-and-potatoes kind of snack.

entry.title: A Nice-Looking Serving Set Will Really Tie Your Table Together
entry.summary: It’s time to stop using regular flatware and cooking utensils.
entry.content:
If you’re the type of person who likes to host, there’s a certain getting-it-together trajectory that occurs in life. When you’re young, you may not care so much about the details: People eating off of different-size plates and drinking wine out of mugs or Mason jars is par for the course. But there comes a point when it’s nice to have a more intentional setup. I’m not saying that everything has to match, or that there are no occasions for disposable goods, or that a formal dining room is required to throw a successful dinner party. But I am saying there are a handful of niceties that help the vibe.

For me, those items have come over time. During the pandemic when I couldn’t travel home, I hosted my first Thanksgiving and traded in my cheap Ikea plates for nicer ones — and since then, for ones I like even more. Last year, I hosted a pretty big holiday dinner and bought a batch of matching linen napkins since the others I owned were all groups of four or six, and I was going for a more formal look. Over the years, I’ve thrifted cheap-but-cute dessert plates (bistro style, but mini) and saved up to buy some high-quality platters and serving bowls.

Serveware was perhaps the last to catch up. It was for some reason a category I didn’t give much thought to until I would put food out for a bunch of people. I always made the situation work with regular cooking utensils and flatware — but honestly, neither of those look great or function great, either too big or too small for most dishes. It’s been relieving to finally feel like I have what I need, whether I’m serving salad, soup, pasta, a braise, roasted vegetables, or a whole chicken — or really, truly anything at all.

While I now own quite a number of serving utensils, there’s one set that I highly recommend as a starting point if you find yourself in the same place I once was. Robert Welch’s Kingham’s stainless-steel pieces are beautifully made in a classic and elegant style that will look good with quite a variety of other tableware. Yes, it’s good to have fun and mix in some other more out-there styles, but these will fit right in, no matter what.

They come in a set of two, three, four, or eight. I own the four-piece, which includes a serving fork, a serving spoon, a slotted serving spoon, and a pastry server. (The largest has an additional bigger spoon, big ladle, small ladle, and butter knife.) It might sound a bit funny to say they work well, but they do: The spoons have nicely shaped bowls with good depth, the tines on the fork easily pierce chunks of meat, the pastry server has a serrated side to cut and is slim enough to easily slide under any slice of dessert. The handles are all comfortable to hold. You can throw them in the dishwasher to clean. And they’re well priced at less than $20 a piece — a very worthwhile investment to help your table feel more considered.

entry.title: The First BEMT Sunscreens Have Landed
entry.summary: The sunscreen filter, which is finally Stateside after many years in Europe and Asia, offers broad UV protection and a lightweight feel.
entry.content:
A few weeks ago, a package from Neutrogena turned up on my doorstep. It featured their latest release of sunscreens and unlike launches past, which contain the same chemical filters I’ve been seeing for a decade with riffs on feel and invisibility, this one had a new filter, bemotrizinol, the first new sunscreen filter approved by the FDA in 27 years. As I wrote about shortly after the announcement, bemotrizinol is a broad-spectrum filter, which protects against both UVA and UVB rays. Most do one or the other. It’s also a bit more stable and degrades slower than the chemical filters we’re used to. That means the time advertised on the bottle is a bit more accurate, so you can be confident about the level of protection you receive. Originally, the ingredient was limited to a single manufacturer, but we’ve seen it popping up in multiple formulas over the past few months.

This is the sunscreen I’ve been testing. It’s reminiscent of the K Beauty sunscreens I’ve tried in that it’s lightweight and nongreasy but still moisturizing. It contains micro-peptide technology to support collagen production and a high SPF factor of 70, protecting against at least 98 percent of UV rays. Another bonus is that it contains antioxidants, which helps to guard against oxidative stress and hyperpigmentation.

There’s also an acne-prone skin version, which is noncomedogenic and has ingredients that help with hyperpigmentation like vitamin E and niacinamide. It’s slightly thinner than the Ultra Sheer formula and sinks in quickly, ideal for wearing under makeup.

Another ultra-lightweight option, this one goes on and disappears near-instantly. It’s packed with antioxidants, including Exo-P, a ferment extract that protects skin from smog and pollution.

Ultra Violette has become a favorite thanks to its skincare-like feel. This is a hybrid formula that contains both physical and chemical filters. Of the available options, this contains the fewest chemical filters with just BEMT, octocrylene and zinc oxide, which the brand says makes it easy to add more actives like pentavitin, a plant-based extract that attracts moisture to the skin. It also has a soft-matte finish, an alternative to the mostly glowy offerings on the market.

entry.title: The 3 Very Best Robot Vacuums for Pets
entry.summary: Hands-off options for staying on top of pet hair.
entry.content:
Last year, my household went from having two small dogs who hardly shed to five dogs. Between the dirt they track in after going outside, the fur the larger three shed, and the occasional turf war that leaves my floors covered in pee, things easily get out of hand. Without a robot vacuum, I’d probably spend half my nights sweeping and scrubbing my floors.

If you have pets, even if your situation isn’t as extreme as mine, you’ll probably find that having a robot vacuum will cut down on the amount of time and effort you spend cleaning up after them. But when it comes to pet messes on your floors, some models are more effective than others. For carpets or rugs, you’ll want a robot vacuum with a good brush that can avoid tangles plus enough suction power to pick up dirt and hair that’s embedded in your carpet or rug’s fibers. But if you have hardwood or tile floors, your pets likely drag dirt and other nasty stuff all across them, so a robot with a mop function might be the way to go.

I’ve tested more than 20 robot vacuums since I started covering them in 2023, including several with mopping capabilities. Because I’ve never not had at least two dogs living with me, every model we’ve recommended has proved to be up to the task of handling a household with pets. In addition, I ran each robot vacuum over my floors at least three times to see how effectively each one avoids random obstacles, such as toys and cables, that your pets may not always leave in the same place. And since none of the five dogs in my home have particularly long fur, I had each vacuum run over some long hairs from a wig and noted whether any tangles resulted and if the vacuum was able to eliminate them. Plus, because pets can be sensitive to noise and it’s often best to run these robots when they aren’t in the room, I also tried out each vacuum’s smart scheduling and single-room cleaning.

Updated on October 30, 2026
I’ve added the Narwal Flow 2 as the new best robot vacuum-mop combo for pets. Everything else is still available and the prices are up to date.

If you have a dog or cat that sheds, it’s important that your robot vacuum’s brushes don’t get stalled by tangled hair (and this is even more important if you have a long-haired pet or household member). Some robot vacs use single brushes, while others have a dual-brush system that digs deep into rug fibers to yank out tough-to-clean gunk. I’ve also seen newer models with single brushes that are split into two parts to better avoid tangles, as well as some with blades that can cut through clumps of pet hair.

Quality brushes don’t just make for a more thorough cleaning; the better the brushes are at sweeping up debris that rests below the surface of a rug or carpet or in crevices, the less suction power the vacuum will have to use. That trade-off can save a lot of battery life, as a vacuum that’s always running at max suction will have to return to the docking station to recharge more frequently, resulting in longer overall cleaning times.

While this wasn’t a huge consideration a few years ago, robot vacuums have significantly more powerful suction now. They still can’t match the suction power of upright or cordless stick vacuums, but they finally have enough power to pick up things that can get stuck deep in the fibers of a rug or carpet — like pet hair. Suction power on robot vacuums is typically measured in pascals (pa) to indicate how much air pressure is being applied. The higher the pa, the more suction power your vacuum’s going to provide.

If you have cats or dogs, there’s a good chance your vacuum will pick up a lot — we mean a lot — of dirt, hair, and other particles. Vacuums with large, self-emptying base stations can hold more dirt than the on-device dustbin, meaning you don’t spend as much time cleaning your robot, and your robot can periodically empty itself throughout a cleaning job to make sure it gets the whole house clean and to keep things running smoothly. You can get models without these base stations for less money, but you’ll have to empty them manually — and frequently.

Run time on a robot vacuum isn’t quite as important as it is with other kinds of vacuums, since a robot has more time to get its cleaning done than you do and it can return to base for a recharge. That said, the longer its run time, the less frequently it’ll have to stop its cleaning job to return to the dock and recharge, meaning you’re more likely to come home to a clean house. Some robots can calculate how much battery they’ll need to finish a cleaning job and only recharge to that percentage, rather than spending more time doing a full recharge. Others will wait to hit 100 percent before resuming cleaning.

Newer vacuums use lasers or cameras to map the layout of your home to avoid obstacles far better than older robots that relied on bumping into things to figure out where they were going. Those that use lasers won’t pick up as many details as those with cameras, as they can’t use object/obstacle detection to avoid things that tend to move around the house unpredictably, like dog or cat toys, bowls, and, in some cases, poop.

On the other hand, laser-based robots without cameras pose fewer privacy risks. They may still save some data about your home, like a blueprint of its layout, but they won’t take any pictures that could contain sensitive information. That doesn’t mean companies don’t work to ensure that their camera-based robots protect your data and your privacy — they do — but if you’re the type to keep a smart speaker out of your home so nobody’s listening, you’re better off with a laser-only robot or one without mapping capabilities.

While companies don’t always publish a lot of details about their filtration systems, we only recommend those with HEPA filters for helping to remove dust, pollen, and pet dander from the air. Those without HEPA filters will simply recirculate those particles around your room and won’t provide as much relief for those with allergies as vacuums with HEPA filters.

Not every home needs a robot with a built-in mop, but they’re worth considering if you have multiple pets. They won’t scrub your floors quite as well as doing it manually (or as well as a dedicated robot mop), but the best robots get about 80 percent of the way there. Most of these robots have two circular pads that are raised until the mopping function is activated so they don’t come into contact with carpets or rugs. They also typically have a self-cleaning function built into their docks that will routinely clean the mopping pads throughout a cleaning job to ensure it isn’t just spreading dirty water across the floor.

Every parent I’ve spoken to about robot vacuums has asked if there are any models with a child lock. Most manufacturers allow you to toggle this mode from the robot’s app.

Brushes: Single-brush system | Suction power: 10,000 pa | Disposal: Self-emptying base station | Run time: 150 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors | Filtration: Yes | Mopping: Yes | Child lock: Yes

Roborock’s Q7 M5+ has enough suction power to pick up clumps of dog or cat hair, the ability to mop, and some of the best smart navigation I’ve seen in a robot. Even with all the bowls, toys, and random items my dogs leave on the floors, it’s managed to avoid nearly every obstacle in its path as well as robots more than double its price, all while leaving my floors notably cleaner.

That’s mostly thanks to Roborock’s intelligent software. It mapped my home in just under half an hour, while other robots took up to 15 minutes longer. Once that’s set up, you can have it run an automatic cleaning job with stock settings or fine-tune things like how much suction the robot’s using, the intensity of the mopping function, and how many times it goes over your floors. You can also schedule cleaning routines, set times where the robot can’t run at all, and put it in child-lock mode so kids can’t turn it on at will.

If your pets tend to spend a lot of time in a particular area — near their bed, food bowls, or play area — you can set custom zones to have the robot target those areas without doing a full cycle through your home. There’s also an option to create no-go zones to avoid any areas where it might get caught up, like near a power strip.

In addition to vacuuming, the Q7 also has a mopping function that’s been good enough to keep my floors tidy despite the constant dirt my dogs track in. Unlike other mopping robots we recommend, however, this one uses a single, non-rotating pad that it pushes down to scrub your floors. It can’t apply as much pressure as robots like the Narwal Flow 2 that have more powerful mops, so it’s not as effective for scrubbing out sticky messes. Additionally, the docking station doesn’t have a cleaning function for the mopping pad, so you’ll have to remove the pad and either clean it by hand or toss it in the washing machine. If you find yourself needing to mop regularly, Narwal’s Flow 2 is worth the extra money.

Brushes: Single brush | Suction power: 31,000 pa | Disposal: Self-emptying base station for dirt and liquid | Run time: 210 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors, camera | Filtration: Yes | Mopping: Yes, hot water cleaning | Child lock: Yes

Narwal’s Flow 2 has enough suction power to yank pet hair out of deep-pile rugs and carpets, and its mopping is so good it has kept my floors squeaky clean despite the best efforts of my five dogs (two of whom love to dig and track in dirt). Especially handy is its ability to automatically detect stains and other messes, then adjust its settings while cleaning that spot, rather than having to run the whole cleaning job at max strength. The newest addition to my fur family isn’t housebroken yet, so I’ve been relying on that feature to clean spots I may have missed while working.

But I don’t have to run a full cleaning job every time my dog has an accident, as you can set custom zones. All you have to do is drag your finger over the portion of the map you want the robot to clean, configure your settings, and let the robot run. Depending on how dirty your pets tend to leave your floors — the more outdoor adventures, walks, or trips to the park, the more outside gunk they’ll likely bring in — you can fine-tune the specifics of your vacuum’s cleaning job. The Flow 2 can be programmed to vacuum and mop your floors from one to three times, and there are options to change the vacuum’s suction power and how much water it uses when mopping. And in addition to smart object detection, this robot also has pet detection, so you don’t have to worry about it charging at your skittish animal.

Beyond being good for managing households with a lot of pet hair, the Flow 2 excels at cleaning up fine particles that can seep into a rug or carpet. For instance, I poured a handful of coffee grounds on my carpet and had the Flow do a quick cleaning job over that spot. After it had run over the spot just once, I couldn’t tell any coffee grounds had been there at all.

Brushes: Single-brush system | Suction power: 3,200 pa | Disposal: Manually emptied bag with diaper salts | Run time: 180 minutes | Smart navigation: Infrared sensors, camera | Filtration: Yes | Mopping: Yes | Child lock: Yes

If you don’t need the Flow 2’s high suction power for things like sucking fur out of deep-pile carpets, the Matic’s more privacy-friendly software, charming design, and smell-free dirt and water bag have made it one of my favorite robots to date.

You can see the Matic’s advantages from the moment you send it to start mapping your home for the first time. Unlike most other robots, which follow a straight pattern when mapping and cleaning your home, the Matic zooms around in a seemingly random pattern. It took a little under 20 minutes to map my home, while other vacuums usually take around 30. Cleaning is almost as quick. In about 45 minutes, it managed to vacuum and mop a week’s worth of dirt and hair while only getting caught once on a loose thread from a rug.

That’s all made possible by Matic’s intelligent software. It’s constantly updating its map based on what it sees as it cleans; the robot’s taller body means its 3-D maps are more detailed than maps from shorter robots. And while most other robots send their mapping data back to a company’s servers — even if that data is anonymized — everything happens locally on the Matic. Despite not feeding into a company’s object-recognition algorithm, this robot is still able to identify messier areas, like a spill on your kitchen floor, and boost its settings for more thorough cleaning.

Especially handy for pet owners: The Matic doesn’t produce the gnarly odor that some other mopping robots do. Many come with a self-emptying dock that stores dirty water after the robot’s on-unit tank gets filled. If you’re not diligent about emptying and cleaning that dock’s tank, it develops a particularly gross smell. That’s not a problem with the Matic. It has a bag inside that stores dirt, debris, and dirty water. To make sure you never have to plug your nose when emptying it, the bag is lined with diaper salts, which kill the odor. So far, I haven’t had any issues.

I do have a few gripes with the Matic. Most importantly for pet owners, its suction is significantly weaker than that of the Saros. It’s fine for pulling hairs off hardwood and short-pile carpets and rugs, but it may struggle with deeper pile rugs. Additionally, its tall body prevents it from reaching places with low clearance, such as underneath a couch or bed. Last, I’ve noticed that it’s not great at reaching the edges of rooms, so you may have to do some spot cleaning from time to time.
