entry.title: The 15 Very Best Women’s Leggings
entry.summary: For running, stretching, and replying to emails.
entry.content:
Whether or not you believe in wearing them outside the house (I wouldn’t judge you either way), leggings should be the most comfortable pair of pants you own. The best ones are stretchy and formfitting without feeling restrictive, and they’re made from high-quality materials that can withstand hundreds of wash and dry cycles without wearing out. To find options for different activities (from lounging to traveling to CrossFit), I spoke with athleisure designers and consultants about which features to look for and which brands to trust. Then I tested out their recommendations for myself. All of the leggings below are stretchy enough to exercise in, but I’ve also written a stand-alone guide to the best yoga pants if you’re spending a lot of time on the mat.

Updated on October 30, 2026
I updated prices and checked stock for all products and added new pairs of leggings from Quince, Athleta, and the Frankie Shop.

Leggings should feel like a second skin when you’ve got them on, so the best brands will offer an extensive size range to ensure that everyone gets a good fit. I’ve noted the available sizing for each of our recommended pairs below.

Leggings are typically constructed from a blend of either nylon and spandex or polyester and spandex. Slightly more durable than polyester, nylon is also more expensive. Polyester is still a great choice and highly effective at wicking sweat away from your skin while exercising.

Elastane (also referred to as spandex or Lycra) is what makes leggings stretchy and comfortable compared to regular pants. “The higher the percentage, the more stretch the fabric will have,” explains Shadi Adada, the co-founder of FittDesign. High-elastane leggings are also more compressive, supporting muscles and enhancing blood flow while you exercise. Most leggings these days claim to have “four-way stretch,” but this is essentially just a marketing term that refers to a high percentage of elastane.

In general, low-compression leggings are best for wearing around the house, medium-compression leggings are great for yoga and Pilates, and high-compression leggings are ideal for running and high-intensity exercise. If you’re exercising (or just prefer a less jiggly look) a percentage of at least 18 percent elastane is ideal, says Souad Acha, co-founder of Stateless Fashion Design and Consulting.

I’ve taken note of whether or not each pair of leggings listed here has pockets. For lounging around at home, walking the dog, or running, pockets are ideal — they “allow you to easily store your keys and phone when you need use of both hands,” says Acha. But yogis I’ve spoken with tend to prefer pocket-free pants. “Anything with extra seams, zippers, or buttons is distracting because you’re rolling around on the floor a lot,” says Sky Ting yoga co-founder Krissy Jones.

Size range: 0 to 14 | Fabric: 81 percent nylon, 19 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: Two side pockets

Lululemon’s leggings are a significant investment but one that I — as well as fellow Strategist staffers and numerous fitness experts we’ve spoken with over the years — have found to be worth it. While the brand’s Wunder Train pants are my favorite for yoga, these Align leggings are thinner and more flexible, which makes them more comfortable to wear while lounging. They’re also ideal maternity wear: Strategist contributing editor Jessica Silvester wore them while seven months pregnant and says the same pair snapped back into shape and still fits her regular proportions years later.

Size range: XS to 3XL | Fabric: 82 percent nylon, 18 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: Waistband pocket, two side pockets

So what’s the difference between $33 and $98 leggings, anyway? The Lululemon Align fabric above looks and feels smoother than Baleaf’s and has stronger lines of reinforced stitching at the seams. But after extensive testing, I’ve found that both brands hold up well in the dryer and will last for years without shrinking or warping in shape. Baleaf’s leggings are affordable yet comfortable, even if they don’t look as nice as expensive brands. As Strategist contributor Maggie Slepian puts it, they’re “right between the compression levels of more supportive tights (which can feel too restrictive for all-day wear) and supersoft leggings (which can sag and lose their shape).” So you can work out in them or work from home in them. Which is not so much the case with ultracompressive leggings that have a higher elastane percentage.

Size range: XXS to 4XL | Fabric: 95 percent cotton, 5 percent elastane (ribbed legging), 90 percent cotton, 10 percent elastane (foldover pant) | Compression: Very low | Pockets: None

I prefer to wear nonathletic leggings around the house — no shiny compression pants while I’m watching Hacks, thanks. If you feel the same, Skims leggings are slinky and comfortable. Fitness guru Tracy Anderson told us she’s obsessed with her cotton ribbed ones: “I wear them with a cashmere sweater — that’s my uniform.” Strategist senior editor Hilary Reid and deputy editor Simone Kitchens prefer the brand’s breezier foldover leggings, which Reid says are “ideal for putting on if I’m rolling out of bed and doing some kind of at-home mat workout in the morning before work.” She adds that while the foldover waistband evokes the early-aughts trends she coveted as a teen, “as a now-30-something, I will say it’s actually kind of utilitarian in that you can adjust the ‘rise’ of the pants depending on how you feel that day.”

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 85 percent polyester, 15 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: Optional

Resident Strategist writer and runner Brenley Goertzen tried on all the leggings from Quince, and these were her favorites because they feel like cotton even though they’re made from a polyester fabric that the brand refers to as Ultra-Soft. “These are my pick if you’re looking for a pair of leggings you can comfortably wear all day, since they are plenty stretchy but also have a brushed, cottonlike softness,” she says. “The extra-thick waistband stays in place nicely, doesn’t dig into my hips, and keeps everything sucked in.”

Size range: XXS to L | Fabric: 87 percent polyester, 13 percent elastane | Compression: Low | Pockets: None

A put-together pair of leggings is hard to find. My fellow Strategist writer Lauren Ro is very particular about wearing athleisure outside the house, and as much as she adores her Lulu Aligns, “they’re slightly too unstructured to comfortably wear around town.” She searched for a pair of leggings with a soft feel that were smoothing and supportive (but not too sporty-looking) and settled on these. “They have a bit more compression than the Aligns without being too tight, giving me more definition and, let’s be honest, confidence,” she says. “I wore them with Spanx’s AirEssentials Half Zip to dim sum with the family and felt like a polished Pilates mom — even though I was unshowered and had bits of har gow in my hair.”

Size range: XXS to 3XL | Fabric: 75 percent polyester, 25 percent elastane | Compression: High | Pockets: One back pocket

Speaking of sweat, these Athleta leggings are made from moisture-wicking polyester along with Lycra, making them optimal for high-intensity exercise. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio picked up her first pair of Elation tights during a Black Friday sale in 2022 and has been wearing them (mainly to work out and coach a girls’ soccer team) ever since. Compared to the Lululemon Aligns, “they are a little more compressive,” she says, as well as thicker. This creates a smoothing effect, and she feels more comfortable wearing them in public. The waistband “never rolls,” and the back waistband pocket will handily fit a smartphone if needed. She owns eight pairs of these in different variations; the Ultra High Rise is her favorite.

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 92 percent cotton, 8 percent elastane | Compression: High | Pockets: Available with or without

This year I went on a quest to find natural-fiber workout gear, which is happily becoming a more mainstream concept as we cut back on global plastic consumption. I was first drawn to Mate’s tights because they both look and feel familiar. Some cotton workout leggings can be a little baggy, but these closely resemble a pair of sleek and compressive polyester yoga pants. The weave is tight and thick enough to mimic a synthetic fabric, the wide waistband compresses your abs, reinforced seams on the sides provide structure, and there’s plenty of stretch. The remarkably smooth cotton sculpts your body somewhat but remains breathable — unlike polyester, which often makes me overheat. I was particularly struck by how well-made these leggings are. There are no loose threads, and the stitching is even. Much more so than other options, they seem explicitly designed for high-intensity workouts. I was able to go running in mine without having to stop and pull them up or adjust the fit and found them just as comfortable as my nylon leggings for Pilates. They did bunch a bit around the ankles; if you’re short like me, definitely opt for the midi rather than full length.

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 77 percent polyester, 23 percent elastane | Compression: High | Pockets: Front and back waistband pockets, side pockets

Goertzen loves these leggings that have streamlined her training sessions by letting her leave the house without a running belt. They have a built-in belt around the waistband with enough space for her phone, keys, gels, AirPods, and even a few treats if she’s jogging with her dog. And there are still two drop-in side pockets on both legs for even more storage. Convenience aside, these are also just a great pair of exercise leggings, with high compression and a tight fabric weave that wicks sweat away from the body.

Size range: XXS to 6XL | Fabric: 79 percent RPET, 11 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | Pockets: One back pocket

I’m not exactly sure how Girlfriend Collective manages to turn plastic bottles into pants, but the result is unusually comfortable and stylish. These yoga pants are a hit among Strategist staffers as well as athletes and yogis we’ve spoken to over the years, including Jones, who calls them “by far the most sustainable” leggings that are “still concerned with fit and look.” Health-care entrepreneur Hil Moss, a breast-cancer survivor who has undergone a mastectomy and rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, says that they made the process just a bit easier: “I have multiple pairs in different colors. That’s how much I love them.”

Size range: XXS to XXL | Fabric: 96 percent acrylic, polyester, and rayon; 4 percent elastane | Compression: Very low | Pockets: None

I like to wear Uniqlo’s Heattech leggings around the house during winter, when central heating is doing most of the work but I still want an extra boost of warmth. They’ve also come in handy while waiting for the Q train in cold and windy subway tunnels. Over the years, numerous fashion insiders have told us that they love their Heattech layers too; celebrity stylist Krisana Sotelo is a fan, and so is Richer Poorer co-founder Iva Pawling, who ran to purchase a pair during an unexpected freezing-cold NYC trip. “They were easy to wear under jeans and saved my built-for-70-degrees self,” she says.

Size range: 2XS to 2XL | Fabric: 74 percent polyamide, 26 percent elastane | Compression: High | ﻿Pockets: None

Strategist contributor Katie Stone, who has tried all the activewear brands, recently did a 180 on Vuori’s popular leggings. She especially recommends this drawstring pair, which she says will stay perfectly positioned during whatever sort of reformer-Pilates gymnastics position you find yourself in. The fabric is thick and structured, so they’re ideal for colder weather and higher impact activities, but the drawstring also means that you can loosen things up a bit when lounging at home.

Size range: XS to XL | Fabric: 90 percent Supplex, 10 percent elastane | Compression: Medium | ﻿Pockets: None

While most leggings are utilitarian-looking at best, Live the Process’s ballet-inspired designs manage to be “shockingly beautiful,” as Jones puts it. “If anyone wants to splurge on the nicest yoga pants out there, their shapes and colors are amazing,” she says. “So is the quality of the material.” Strategist senior writer Liza Corsillo, who has been wearing the same pair of Live the Process leggings for close to a decade, agrees. The brand’s stirrup leggings were first recommended to me by dancer Angela Trimbur, who came across them while receiving breast-cancer treatments a few years ago. “I spent a lot of time at home resting in blah-looking basics that left me feeling extra blah,” she recalls. “I realized that investing in chicer looks to rest in made me feel more confident, hopeful, and happy.” These days, she wears them while dancing in her home studio and then tosses street clothes over the top to run errands.

Size range: XXS to XL | Fabric: 100 percent merino wool | Compression: Low | ﻿Pockets: None

When Strategist contributing writer Laura Neilson went on a skeptical hunt for the best stirrup leggings, she fell in love with this ribbed pair from the Frankie Shop. She’s always “genuinely excited” to wear them because they’re made entirely from merino wool, which gives them “the same pull-on ease as a beloved ribbed turtleneck.” This means that they’re most ideal for lounging around in when it’s sweater weather and shouldn’t be worn for exercise. “I’d wear them for weekend errands as a stylish alternative to sweatpants, maybe with an oversize chunky sweater,” Neilson adds.

Flared yoga pants are both trendy and versatile; what I especially like about Alo’s Airbrush ones is that they’re constructed from a soft and stretchy matte fabric rather than the more traditional shiny yoga-pant material. This means they really do work as (very comfortable and flattering) everyday pants if you throw a T-shirt over the top. I tried both the flared and bootcut styles and would advise the latter if you favor a subtle ’90s look over a more billowy ’70s one.

entry.title: Jones Road’s Color Corrector Is the Difference Between Good and Great Makeup
entry.summary: It’s one more step, but it makes a huge difference in your makeup.
entry.content:
For years, color correcting was one of those makeup techniques that I knew I should do but never did. It always seemed a bit advanced for my otherwise simple makeup routine and just one more step in the process. Then Jones Road launched a color corrector this fall — Wide Awake Brightening Neutralizer — along with its new Wide Awake Brightening Concealer, a separate product that is meant to be applied before the concealer to correct discoloration. Fine, I’ll try it, I thought, because I typically like Jones Road products. When I looked back at pictures from the event I wore it to, I could see that my skin tone looked more cohesive and my makeup looked more finished than it usually does. Since then, I’ve been color correcting my under eyes regularly and also dabbing the product on broken capillaries around my face before using concealer and foundation.

I suspect I’m not alone here. Most makeup wearers are probably not color correcting before concealer or foundation because it just seems too pro-level or maybe even intimidating, but it’s work worth doing, says makeup artist Daniel Martin. I asked him to break down and demystify the technique.

Most people don’t have just one tone on their face. We may have darkness under the eyes, redness around the nose or on the cheeks, or darker patches on parts of the face, and foundation isn’t necessarily going to cover it all. You may be thinking, But isn’t that what concealer is for? Yes, and concealers may cover discoloration, but sometimes those underlying blue, purple, or red areas still show through. A color corrector counteracts that tone before you add coverage. Martin admits it’s precision work, but it’s an additional step that ultimately makes the rest of your makeup look better. “If you’re someone who has dark under eyes, that’s where you want to spend your most time,” he says. “Once that’s perfected and blended, everything else is pretty easy.”

This is the intimidating part for many people, but it’s basic color theory. Color correctors come in a range of shades, including pinks, peaches, apricots, yellows, and greens. Most people benefit from a peachy tone (ranging from light to dark peaches) under the eyes, which neutralizes purply blue tones. Deep apricots are also helpful for gray tones or brown spots. It’s often said that green is best for counteracting redness, but Martin isn’t a fan. “They’re sometimes too green,” he says. Instead, he uses yellow on redness. “The yellow and red of your skin creates an orange or a peach tone, and I like bringing more warmth to the skin.”

For me, the texture of the corrector makes a difference. I’ve tried some liquid correctors that seemed too wet and slippery and just mixed in with the concealer. Hours later, I could see the peach tone under my eyes. The Jones Road neutralizer is creamy but not wet and easy to pat onto the skin without slipping around too much. Martin says the texture is really a matter of preference, and skin prep plays a bigger role in how it applies and layers.

As mentioned, skin prep matters a lot here. When I told Martin about my “too wet” corrector, he suspected that I didn’t allow the emollients in my eye cream to sink in first. So allow at least five minutes after applying serums and moisturizers before going in with a corrector. Martin likes to use his fingers, not a brush, to correct. “I like to use the heat from my hands to lay the product and keep it from looking dry or cakey,” he says. “You want it to meld; you don’t want it to just sit on your skin.” He then adds concealer and foundation. For stubborn discoloration, Martin will then go back in with the corrector over the foundation, too, and finish with a light dusting of powder to set.

This is the one I’ve been applying. It comes in nine different shades. I’m using Light Peachy Pink, which is the perfect, not-too-pink-not-too-peach shade that’s just right for my light skin.

“I recently used this on actor Naomi Akie,” says Martin. “It’s made for the eyes, but I wound up using it to correct all over her face. The dry-down was quick.”

“Huda Beauty has a nice corrector that I just started using,” says Martin. “It’s pretty wet, but the pigment dries down really fast. You can get a trial size at Sephora, which is nice if you don’t want to commit to a big one yet.”

entry.title: A Gift for Every Type of Wife
entry.summary: Picks for every type of wife at every price point.
entry.content:
The closer the relationship you have with someone, the more pressure there is to find the right gift. So, if you’re shopping for your wife, I imagine you’re sweating. Whether you’re a newlywed trying to nail it, someone trying to say “I love you as co-parent but also as a person,” or a pair who’s been gifting for so long you’ve resorted to really scraping the barrel, it seemingly never gets easier. That’s why I’m here to help.

I’ve combed the Strategist archives, rummaged through my mental Rolodex, and also interviewed many tasteful, stylish wives in order to put together a list of gift ideas. I’ve covered a lot of bases here, so all manner of wives (from those in marathon training to wives who have a tinned-fish obsession) are catered to. My forever gifting philosophy is to mix highbrow and lowbrow. Stuff a Coach bag full of her favorite childhood candy! Get her a fancy stand mixer to go along with a new cookbook! Or perhaps some absurdly luxurious pajamas to pair with a restock of fluffy socks. You know her the best!
